newsitem.title: USA: Scientists say New World settled 12,500 years ago.
newsitem.headline: Scientists say New World settled 12,500 years ago.

text.p: A team of U.S. scientists said on Monday they have evidence proving that humans lived in what is now southern Chile 12,500 years ago, effectively pushing back settlement of the New World by 1,300 years.

The archaeologists said the artifacts found at the Monte Verde site about 500 miles (800 km) south of Santiago include remnants of hide covered huts, a child's footprint, finely crafted tools of bone and tusk and more than 700 stone tools.

The team, which visited the site for 10 days last month, told a news conference in Dallas that detailed analysis of layers of sediment where the artifacts were found showed that they are 12,500 years old.
Archaeologists had previously believed humans first spread into the New World 11,200 years ago in a period known as the "Clovis horizon".
"It's hard to overstate the importance of the team's consensus," said Alex Barker, curator of archaeology at the Dallas Museum of Natural History, which helped fund the expedition.
"For 60 years, the Clovis-period entry of humans into the New World has withstood all challenges. Now the Monte Verde site establishes that humans arrived earlier," Barker said.
He said the team of scientists included experts who had worked at Monte Verde for years as well as sceptics.
If confirmed, the findings would force a radical change in standing theories on how humans migrated to the New World.

Until now, most archaeologists have thought humans first settled the New World by crossing the Bering land bridge that linked Alaska to Asia 12,000 years ago, when sea levels were lower, and then spread slowly southwards through the Americas.
The human artifacts at Monte Verde were preserved because a nearby creek backed up and buried the abandoned village in a peat bog for thousands of years.
The scientists who gathered to announce their findings did not put forward a theory on exactly how the settlers arrived at Monte Verde.
It is not the first time scientists have claimed to have found sites in the Americas dating back to beyond the Clovis period, but all previous claims were later proven to be false.

"All of the numerous pre-Clovis sites proposed through the decades have had a shadow over them. The Monte Verde conclusion is as definitive as archaeology gets," said George Stuart, chief archaeologist at the National Geographic Society.
